description: Renewable and non-renewable energy sources, fossil fuels, and how products store energy.
content_html:
Energy in Design and Technology

Every product requires energy to manufacture, and many require energy to use. Designers must understand where energy comes from and how it is stored, because these choices affect a product’s sustainability, cost and practicality. Energy sources fall into two broad categories: renewable energy and non-renewable energy.

Renewable Energy Sources

Solar (photovoltaic): Photovoltaic (PV) cells convert sunlight directly into electricity. Silicon-based PV cells are the most common. Solar panels on buildings and integrated into products (calculators, garden lights) reduce dependence on mains power. Efficiency of commercially available panels typically ranges from around 15–22% for silicon cells.

Wind: Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of moving air to spin a generator. Onshore turbines are cheaper to build and maintain; offshore turbines benefit from stronger and more consistent winds. Wind power is intermittent — output depends on wind speed — so energy storage is needed to smooth supply.

Hydroelectric: Water flowing through a turbine — usually in a dam — generates electricity. Hydroelectric power is reliable and controllable, but requires a suitable geographical location and raises environmental concerns about the habitat flooded by reservoirs.

Geothermal: Heat from the Earth’s crust is used to generate steam that drives turbines or to heat buildings directly. Practically available in regions with volcanic activity, such as Iceland, but less so in the UK.

Biomass: Organic material — wood, crop waste, dedicated energy crops — is burned or fermented to release energy. It is considered low-carbon (the CO₂ released was recently absorbed by the growing plant), but combustion still produces particulates and other pollutants.

Wave and tidal: The movement of ocean waves and tidal flows can drive turbines. The UK’s coastal location makes these sources potentially significant, but the technology is less mature and more expensive than wind or solar at present.

Key Fact

The six main renewable energy sources covered in this course are: solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, and wave/tidal. All are replenished naturally, but most are intermittent or location-dependent — requiring storage or grid balancing to be practically useful.

Non-Renewable Energy Sources

Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — were formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms. Burning them releases the carbon stored in them as CO₂, contributing to the greenhouse effect and climate change. They are energy-dense and have well-established distribution infrastructure, which is why they still supply the majority of global energy.

Nuclear power is sometimes described as ‘low carbon’ because it does not burn fuel. Uranium atoms are split in a process called fission, releasing large amounts of heat used to generate steam and electricity. Nuclear power produces a reliable baseload of electricity without direct CO₂ emissions, but generates radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years, and carries a small risk of catastrophic accidents.

The following table compares key characteristics:

Feature Fossil fuels Renewables (e.g. solar/wind)
AvailabilityFinite; will run outContinuously replenished
CO₂ emissionsHighLow to zero during operation
ReliabilityOn-demand (energy-dense)Often intermittent (wind/solar)
InfrastructureWell-establishedExpanding rapidly

Energy Storage for Products and Manufacturing

Many products need to store energy so they can be used without a permanent connection to the mains. The main storage methods are:

Batteries are the most common energy storage for portable products. Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries power smartphones, laptops and electric vehicles because of their high energy density and long cycle life. Non-rechargeable alkaline batteries are used in lower-drain products such as TV remotes. Battery disposal is an environmental concern — lithium and other metals require specialist recycling.

Mains electricity powers most manufacturing equipment and large household appliances. It is reliable and effectively unlimited in supply, but the carbon intensity of the grid depends on how the electricity was generated — a factory powered by renewable electricity has a lower carbon footprint than one on coal-sourced power.

Wind-up mechanisms store mechanical energy in a spring. Traditionally used in clockwork mechanisms and wind-up toys, they are now applied in products for regions without reliable electricity — such as wind-up radios and torches designed for off-grid use in developing countries. The Freeplay wind-up radio is a well-known example of this approach applied for social good.

Key Fact

Lithium-ion batteries are preferred for portable and high-drain applications because of their high energy density (they store a lot of energy per unit of weight) and long cycle life (they can be recharged hundreds or thousands of times). Alkaline batteries have lower energy density and cannot be recharged.

PV cells can be integrated directly into products to provide power without batteries or mains connection. Applications include: solar-powered calculators (very low power draw — even indoor light is sufficient); garden lighting (PV cell charges a battery during the day, powers LEDs at night); and building-integrated PV panels on roofs and facades. In wearable technology, flexible thin-film PV cells are being embedded into clothing and backpack fabric, though efficiency remains lower than rigid silicon cells. The key design consideration is surface area: PV cells must be exposed to light, which affects the form and orientation of the product.
exam_tip_html: Energy questions often ask you to ‘compare’ or ‘discuss’ renewable and non-renewable sources. Always link each source to a specific advantage and limitation — for example, solar is clean and silent but intermittent; nuclear is reliable and low-carbon but produces radioactive waste. For storage questions, name the storage method and explain why it suits the product: ‘a lithium-ion battery is used because of its high energy density, allowing the device to operate for many hours without recharging.’
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, wave/tidal) are replenished naturally but are often intermittent; non-renewable sources (coal, oil, gas, nuclear) are energy-dense but finite or produce problematic waste.
  • Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight to electricity and can be integrated into products; lithium-ion batteries provide high energy density for portable and high-drain applications; wind-up mechanisms store mechanical energy for off-grid use.
  • In the exam, always link each energy source to a specific advantage and a real limitation — and link each storage method to why it suits the product it powers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following energy sources is non-renewable?
A) Solar
B) Biomass
C) Natural gas
D) Hydroelectric
State two advantages of using solar (photovoltaic) cells to power a garden lighting product.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per advantage (any two):
• No running cost once installed (no mains electricity needed)
• No direct CO2 emissions during operation
• No wiring required — can be placed anywhere with sufficient sunlight
• Battery can be charged during the day and power lights at night
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a wind-up mechanism stores and releases energy in a product.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Turning the winding key stores mechanical (potential) energy in a coiled spring (1).
• When released, the spring uncoils and transfers kinetic energy to the mechanism (1).
• This energy can drive a generator to produce electricity or directly power moving parts (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose to power a portable music device using a lithium-ion battery rather than disposable alkaline batteries.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• Lithium-ion batteries have a higher energy density than alkaline batteries (1), meaning the device can operate for longer between charges without increasing the product’s size or weight (1).
• Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable and can complete hundreds of charge cycles (1), reducing running costs and the number of batteries sent to landfill compared with single-use alkaline cells (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer of children's toys is deciding whether to power its products using disposable batteries or rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. Explain, with reference to energy storage and sustainability, which option a designer would be justified in recommending.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed argument for the justified recommendation, with specific reference to energy density, rechargeability, lifecycle cost and disposal/recycling implications for both types. The toy context is embedded (e.g. child-safe charging, product lifespan).
Secure: Both options considered with developed points; recommendation clearly linked to sustainability and storage properties.
Developing: Basic comparison made; sustainability mentioned but not specifically linked to storage type.
Emerging: Simple statements about batteries being better or worse; minimal technical reasoning.
[6 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using wind power as an energy source for national electricity generation compared with nuclear power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation covering wind advantages (renewable, zero emissions during operation, scalable, no radioactive waste) and disadvantages (intermittent, visual impact, noise, requires storage or grid balancing), versus nuclear advantages (reliable baseload, low direct emissions, high energy density) and disadvantages (radioactive waste, long construction time, accident risk, high decommissioning cost). Weighted judgement reached.
Secure: At least two developed points per source; judgement present.
Developing: Points mostly listed without development; one side stronger than the other.
Emerging: Simple pros/cons with minimal explanation; no judgement.
[8 marks — levels-based]

options: Store electrical energy in a chemical form for later use
Convert the kinetic energy of wind into electricity
Convert sunlight directly into electrical energy
Use heat from the Earth's crust to generate steam

knowledge_checks.q: Which energy storage method works by coiling a spring to store mechanical energy?
Fossil fuels are described as non-renewable because they exist in _____ quantities and cannot be replaced once used.
Lithium-ion batteries are preferred for portable devices because of their high energy _____ and long cycle life.
Match each energy source to its key characteristic:
right: Uses flowing water through a dam to drive turbines — reliable but location-dependent
Burns organic material; considered low-carbon but produces combustion pollutants
Splits uranium atoms by fission; reliable and low-carbon but produces radioactive waste

flashcard_questions.q: What is a renewable energy source?
flashcard_questions.a: One that is naturally replenished and will not run out on a human timescale.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a non-renewable energy source?
flashcard_questions.a: One that exists in finite quantities and cannot be replaced once used.
Sunlight directly into electrical energy using semiconductor materials.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is wind power described as intermittent?
flashcard_questions.a: Output depends on wind speed, so electricity generation varies and cannot be controlled on demand.

flashcard_questions.q: What energy source does a hydroelectric power station use?
flashcard_questions.a: The kinetic energy of flowing water through a dam, driving a turbine.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is biomass considered low-carbon compared with fossil fuels?
flashcard_questions.a: The CO2 released was recently absorbed by the growing plant, unlike ancient carbon in fossil fuels.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main environmental disadvantage of nuclear power?
flashcard_questions.a: It generates radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles rather than alkaline batteries?
flashcard_questions.a: They have higher energy density and can be recharged hundreds of times.

flashcard_questions.q: What kind of energy does a wind-up mechanism store?
flashcard_questions.a: Mechanical (potential) energy in a coiled spring.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one product designed for off-grid use that uses a wind-up mechanism.
flashcard_questions.a: The Freeplay wind-up radio, designed for use in areas without reliable electricity.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must battery disposal be handled carefully?
flashcard_questions.a: Lithium and other battery metals require specialist recycling and can be harmful if landfilled.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the carbon intensity of mains electricity vary?
flashcard_questions.a: It depends on how the electricity was generated — renewable sources produce lower-carbon electricity than coal.

glossary_terms.definition: Energy sources that are replenished naturally and will not run out on a human timescale, such as solar, wind and hydroelectric power.
Energy sources that exist in finite quantities and cannot be replaced once used, such as coal, oil and natural gas.
Devices that convert sunlight directly into electrical energy using semiconductor materials.
